cards.front: {{c1::Trait frequency}} is how common a trait is in a population, often given as a percent.
cards.quote: Trait frequency is how common a trait is in a population, often given as a percent.

cards.front: An {{c1::environment}} is everything around a living thing, such as bark, air, food and predators.
cards.quote: An environment is everything around a living thing, such as bark, air, food and predators.

cards.front: What is natural selection?
cards.back: The process in which individuals whose inherited traits suit their environment are more likely to survive and reproduce, so those traits become more common over generations.
cards.quote: Natural selection is the process in which individuals whose inherited traits suit their environment are more likely to survive and reproduce, so those traits become more common over generations.

cards.front: In natural selection, what changes: one moth or the whole population? Explain.
cards.back: The population. Natural selection changes how common a trait is across a population, not any one moth.
cards.quote: It changes trait frequency in a population, not any one moth.

cards.front: Why can the model of moths on sooty bark be called a simplification?
cards.back: In the model, survivors have young of their own colour. A real moth gets colour genes from both parents.
cards.quote: That is a simplification: a real moth gets colour genes from both parents.
cards.section: Explore: be the birds that hunt moths

cards.front: Some individuals may move away, which changes a population in a different way, called {{c1::gene flow}}.
cards.quote: Some individuals may move away, which changes the population in a different way, called gene flow.

cards.front: In biology, what does "fit" mean in "survival of the fittest"? Does it mean strongest?
cards.back: Fit means well suited to the environment and able to leave offspring. It does not mean strongest.
cards.quote: In biology, fit means well suited to the environment and able to leave offspring. It does not mean strongest.

cards.front: Do birds choose which moths breed? Explain how birds still cause natural selection.
cards.back: No. Birds only find some moths more often. Moths that are found less often survive and have more young.
cards.why: A dark moth on sooty bark is fit because birds miss it more often.
cards.quote: Birds never choose which moths breed; they only find some moths more often.

cards.front: In the moth model, you make the birds less sharp-eyed. Will the percent of dark moths on sooty bark change faster or slower?
cards.back: Slower. When birds miss more moths of both colours, matching the bark gives a smaller advantage.
cards.quote: When birds miss more moths of both colours, matching the bark gives a smaller advantage.
cards.section: Explore: be the birds that hunt moths

cards.front: A wood has a few rare, inherited dark moths and many pale moths on pale, lichen-covered bark. Soot then kills the lichen and darkens the bark. What happens to the percent of dark moths over generations, and why?
cards.back: It rises. Birds are more likely to find pale moths, so dark moths have more young and become common.
cards.quote: So dark moths had more young and became common.

cards.front: In a wood where dark moths had become common, the air gets cleaner and lichen grows back on the bark. What happens to the pale form, and why?
cards.back: The pale form tends to become common again, as it did in Britain and parts of the United States. Birds find dark moths more easily on pale bark, so pale moths survive and have more young.
cards.quote: The pale form became common again in Britain and parts of the United States.

cards.front: What is artificial selection?
cards.back: People choosing which plants or animals breed.
cards.quote: The second film showed artificial selection: people choosing which plants or animals breed.

cards.front: How do natural and artificial selection differ in what affects who breeds? Give one example of each.
cards.back: Natural selection: conditions such as predators or weather, for example dark moths on sooty bark. Artificial selection: people's choices, for example dog breeds or corn.
cards.quote: Corn came from a wild grass called teosinte, after farmers kept seeds from the plants they liked best.

cards.front: What is an adaptation?
cards.back: A structure, function or behaviour that comes from natural selection and helps an organism survive and reproduce.
cards.quote: An adaptation is a structure, function or behaviour that comes from natural selection and helps an organism survive and reproduce.

cards.front: Why is weight lost from hunger not an adaptation?
cards.back: It comes from one animal's experience, not from inherited traits shaped over generations.
cards.quote: It comes from one animal's experience, not from inherited traits shaped over generations.

cards.front: How is natural selection related to evolution?
cards.back: Evolution is a change in the inherited traits of a population from one generation to the next. Natural selection is one cause of evolution, and the one that produces adaptations.
cards.quote: Natural selection is one cause of evolution, and the one that produces adaptations.

cards.front: A breeder wants chickens that lay more eggs. Each year she lets only the hens that lay the most eggs have chicks. Is this natural or artificial selection, and what happens to the flock over generations?
cards.back: Artificial selection, because she chooses which hens breed.
cards.why: People use the same idea as natural selection, with their own choice in place of the environment.
cards.quote: Key idea: Adaptations come from natural selection, people use the same idea in artificial selection, and natural selection is one cause of evolution.

cards.front: In 2002, 162 of 706 pale moths and 31 of 101 dark moths were eaten or missing. About what percent of each colour was eaten or missing, and which colour lost the larger share?
cards.back: Pale: 162 / 706 is about 23%. Dark: 31 / 101 is about 31%. Dark lost the larger share.
cards.why: Birds removed a larger share of dark moths than of pale moths.
cards.quote: Pale: about 23%. Dark: about 31%, the larger share.

cards.front: In the Madingley light-trap data, dark moths were 12 percent of moths caught in 2001 and 1 percent in 2007. By how many percentage points did the dark form drop?
cards.back: 12 - 1 = 11 percentage points.
cards.quote: Subtract the endpoint percentages: 12 − 1 = 11 percentage points.

cards.front: In the Madingley moth counts from 2001 to 2007, one year broke the downward trend in dark moths. What happened, and does it change the overall conclusion?
cards.back: The value rose from 6% to 7% in 2004, then fell again. The dark form still became less common across the full seven-year record.
cards.quote: The dark form became less common across the full seven-year record, with a small rise in 2004.

cards.front: Dark moths in light-trap samples, 2001 to 2007, were 12, 10, 6, 7, 4, 2 and 1 percent of moths caught. What is the mean percent?
cards.back: The seven values add to 42. 42 / 7 = 6, so the mean is 6%.
cards.quote: Add the seven percentages to get 42, then divide by 7. The mean is 6%.

cards.front: A student tests whether background colour changes which paper moths a classmate finds first, using 20 white and 20 black paper moths on white and black sheets. Name the independent and dependent variables, and two things to keep the same.
cards.back: Independent: the background (white or black sheet). Dependent: how many moths of each colour are picked up. Keep the same, for example, moth size and shape, the number of each colour, picking time of 10 seconds, or distance of 1 metre.
cards.quote: The independent variable is the background: a sheet of white paper or a sheet of black paper, each 50 centimetres by 50 centimetres.

cards.front: In the paper moth model, fewer black moths are picked on black paper and fewer white moths on white paper. What does this show, and what does it not yet show about real moths?
cards.back: Background matching makes the paper moths harder to find. It does not show that this helps real moths survive. Field experiments with birds test that.
cards.quote: If fewer black moths are picked on black paper, and fewer white moths on white paper, background matching makes the paper moths harder to find.

cards.front: Write a claim, with evidence and reasoning, about how the change in the environment changed the dark peppered moth population near Cambridge, England.
cards.back: Claim: the dark form became less common. Evidence: dark moths fell from about 12% of moths caught in 2001 to about 1% in 2007, and birds removed a larger share of dark moths (about 31%) than pale (about 23%) in 2002. Reasoning: on cleaner, paler bark birds find dark moths more easily, so they leave fewer young.
cards.quote: The whole experiment pointed the same way: birds removed a larger share of dark moths than of pale moths.
